title: 200 core words
hook: a day that stings, then tilts back: the Gita's two words for how a day lands
tomorrow: what did the thunder say, three times?

segments.voice: Yesterday, 200 core words went to the roots: kri, doing; bhu, being; gam, going. Today, two words for how a day lands.

A text that says can we talk. A grade lower than expected. Feedback that stings more than it should. None of it is a crisis, and all of it lands. Then, a few hours later, a good song, a funny message, and the day tilts back. By evening it's hard to say whether it was a good day or a bad one. Krishna has a line for that tilting, in the Gita's second chapter, and two core words sit in it: sukha and duhkha.
screen: `A DAY THAT STINGS.` → `A DAY THAT TILTS BACK.` → `SUKHA AND DUHKHA.`

segments.voice: Sukha: ease, happiness, things going well. Duhkha: pain, sorrow, things going badly. The Gita sets them side by side more than once. In 2.14, Krishna calls Arjuna by his mother's name, Kaunteya, son of Kunti, and tells him: the touches of the senses bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come, and they go. They don't last. Bear them patiently. Cold and heat are a plain picture: nobody argues with weather, and nobody expects it to stay. The word for bear them is titikshasva: endure, let it be hard for a while. The word for them is agamapayinah, the coming-and-going ones, and it's two words melted at an a, just like the joins from last week: agama, coming, and apayin, going away. Then the next verse. The steady person, the same in sukha and duhkha, whom these don't shake, is fit for the deathless. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the sting isn't real, or that the good song doesn't matter. Cold is cold. A hard note from a teacher stings, and that's allowed. It says both come and go. A reader can learn sukha and duhkha in a minute. Holding them evenly takes longer. That's what Arjuna is being offered, standing between two armies: not numbness, but steadiness under a feeling that will pass.
screen: `SUKHA: EASE. DUHKHA: PAIN.` · `THEY COME, AND THEY GO.` · `AGAMA + APAYIN.` · `STEADY IN BOTH.` · then, large: `NOT NUMB: STEADY.`

segments.voice: Sit with the hands resting open on the knees or thighs, palms up. Let something from this week that stung rest in one hand, and something good in the other, and keep both hands equally still. If the sting pulls one hand into a fist, open it again, gently. Let the breath come and go, the way the verse says they do.
Two hundred core words, plain and returning. Today, sukha, ease, and duhkha, pain: a pair that comes and goes. They arrive together, so learn them together.
Pocket this: 200 core words, and ease and pain both come and go. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: your team loses the final after a great season. a teammate says, 'nothing matters anyway.' what fits Gita 2.14?
options: it stings, and it'll pass: bear it without letting it shake you.

fork.reveal: the verse doesn't deny the sting. pleasure and pain come and go; the steady one bears them without being shaken.

original.note: Sanskrit: ease and pain, the Gita's coming-and-going pair.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita tells you to feel nothing.
what it means: sukha and duhkha come and go; the steady person bears them evenly.
what a scholar hears: matrasparshah, the senses' touches; agamapayinah, agama + apayin; titikshasva, endure (Gita 2.14), and samaduhkhasukham in 2.15.
recall: to be; the root list opens with it

chat.meaning: Gita 2.14: pleasure and pain come and go; bear them patiently. Steadiness, not pretending the sting isn't there.

Kaunteya.meaning: son of Kunti: a name for Arjuna
